text: (c) Καὶ τὴν προχείρησιν. Quo etiam modo unus et alter Vatic. etsi Baronio editum προχείρισιν· redditque Turrianus promptitudinem, quasi Maximus vocem voce explicet, vel sic Monothelitæ explicarent. Nam certe habitus, ἕξις promptitudo est et habilitas, sic nobis actibus acquisita et exercitatione. Verum ipse Maximus sequentibus sese explicat, cum ad explanandum ὁμωνυμίαν vocis αὐτεξουσιότητος, in Deo, et angelis et hominibus, discrimen affert liberæ facultatis in angelis et in nobis, quod in angelis cum habitu concurrit προχείρησις, nulla interjecta temporis mora: ipsa scilicet aggressio, et conatus: in nobis vero præintelligatur habitus tempore aggressioni; ac, si vis, usui, quod ea vox propius sonare videtur: quod sit quasi in promptu, et expeditum. Deus certe, ὑπερουσίως, suum ipse intelligere et velle: Angeli νόες, semper in actu intelligendi atque volendi; nos in actu ex potentia, nec continue. Sicque Nestoriani nostro, aliorumque sanctorum et prophetarum more, in quorum ordinem Christum cogebant, sola in eo excellentia ei concessa; in quam ipsam foveam Monothelitæ expositione sua Maximo confutata proruebant.
anchorLine: θήσεως ποιεῖται τὴν ἕξιν καὶ τὴν προχείρησιν (c)·
en: On 'and the προχείρησις': In this way, too, one and another Vatican manuscript, although Baronius's edition has προχείρισιν, and Turrianus rendered it 'promptitude', as if Maximus were explaining a word by the same word, or as the Monothelites would explain it. For habitus (ἕξις) is certainly promptitude and aptitude, acquired in us by acts and exercise. But Maximus himself explains himself in what follows, when, to clarify the homonymy of the word αὐτεξουσιότης in God, in angels and in men, he brings out the difference of free capacity in angels and in us: in angels the προχείρησις concurs with the habit with no interval of time, that is, the very undertaking and endeavour; in us the habit is understood as preceding the undertaking in time; and, if you wish, the word seems to sound closer to use, since it is as if at hand and ready. God, certainly, supersubstantially, has his own understanding and willing; angels, as minds, are always in the act of understanding and willing; we are in act out of potency, and not continuously. And thus our Nestorian [opponents], following the custom of other saints and prophets, into whose order they were forcing Christ, with excellence alone granted to him; into which very pit the Monothelites, by their own exposition, ran headlong, refuted by Maximus.

text: (d) Τὸ σῶμα ἅπτεται. Locus vexatissimus, ad astruendam propriam corporis actionem, ac functionem, qua ipse Dominus miracula operaretur, ut unitione vivificatricem carnem effectam ostenderet, ut passim Cyrillus et alii Patres. Est ergo, Tangit corpus; plana allusione ad locum margini ascriptum; mirorque quid Turriano in mentem venerit, quod reddit, corpus tangitur; cum ἅπτομαι passive sit ab ἅπτω, quod est accendere; fuissetque illi reddendum, corpus uritur. Sed quod sequitur, δι᾽ ἀμφοτέρων φεύγει τὸ πάθος, redditque, utrisque fugit passionem, longe absurdius, nec dignum viro Theologo. Quæ enim hæc cohæsio, quæ lumina? Fugit passio, morbus, lepra. Habet catena Regia quæ fuit card. Mazar. Luc. v, ex qua in supplemento meo apposui Dom. i. post Oct. Epiphaniæ. Locus sumptus est ex orat. 1 in Dominicam resurrectionem, etsi ibi Græca edita mutila, quæ ipsa Franciscus Zinus integra habuit. Sunt vero hæc: Προσέρχεται ὁ λεπρὸς διερρυηκὼς καὶ ἠχρειωμένος τῷ σώματι. Πῶς γίνεται ἐπὶ τούτου παρὰ τοῦ Κυρίου ἴασις; Ἡ ψυχὴ θέλει καὶ τὸ σῶμα ἅπτεται, καὶ δι᾽ ἀμφοτέρων φεύγει πάθος. Ἀπῆλθε γάρ, φησίν, ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ παραχρῆμα ἡ λέπρα. Fr. Zinus ita reddebat: Accedit leprosus dissolutus, atque confectus. Quomodo curatur a Domino? Animus vult, corpus tangit: utroque modo expellitur morbus. Statim enim, ut scriptum est, discessit ab eo lepra; Luc. v, 18. Si quis male officiosorum typorum culpam velit, potius quam Turriani, pugnare nolim.
anchorLine: τοῦ Κυρίου· Ἡ ψυχὴ θέλει, τὸ σῶμα ἅπτεται (d)·
en: On 'the body touches': A most vexed passage, [adduced] to establish the body's own action and function, by which the Lord himself worked miracles, to show the flesh made life-giving by the union, as Cyril and other Fathers say throughout. So the sense is 'the body touches', a plain allusion to the place written in the margin. I wonder what came into Turrianus's mind when he rendered it 'the body is touched', since ἅπτομαι is passive of ἅπτω, which means 'to kindle'; and he ought to have rendered it 'the body is burned'. But what follows, 'by both the passion flees', he renders 'by both it flees the passion', which is far more absurd and unworthy of the Theologian. What coherence is that, what light? What flees is the passion, the sickness, the leprosy. The Regia catena, once Cardinal Mazarin's, has Luke v, from which I set out in my supplement for the first Sunday after the Octave of Epiphany. The passage is taken from Oration 1 on the Sunday of the Resurrection, though the Greek printed there is mutilated; Franciscus Zinus had it whole. It runs: 'The leper approaches, wasted and ruined in body. How does the healing come about in his case from the Lord? The soul wills and the body touches, and through both the passion flees. For, he says, the leprosy left him immediately.' Franciscus Zinus rendered it thus: 'The leper comes, wasted and worn out. How is he cured by the Lord? The mind wills, the body touches: the sickness is driven out in both ways. For at once, as it is written, the leprosy departed from him' (Luke v, 18). If anyone wishes to blame the careless printers rather than Turrianus, I would not quarrel.

text: (e) Ἀλλ᾽ ἡ θέλησις, ἡ βούλησις. Dictum istud Athanasio, l. De incarnat. Christi, p. 631, ad eum locum Pauli Rom. xi. Τίς ἔγνω νοῦν Κυρίου; Subjungit enim, νοῦς Κυρίου, οὔπω Κύριος· ἀλλὰ Κυρίου θέλησις, ἡ βουλή (sic enim ibi editum) ἡ ἐνέργεια πρός τι. Quibus significat, eam vocem Paulo, non esse ipsum Dominum, et quam Apolinaristæ subsistentem in eo divinam Mentem volebant; seu Verbum, quod in ipso mentis officium impleret; sed vim ipsam voluntatis et intelligendi, seu etiam agendi ad aliquid relatam. Locus Clementis 6. illo Strom. non occurrit, nisi sua prolixitate oculum fugit. Βούλησιν velle videtur, quæ sit certo judicio de aliquo; idcirco εὔλογος ὄρεξις, nec longe abest ἡ βουλή, potuitque Athanasius alteram alterius loco vocem usurpare. In Deo βουλή, sine imperfectione accipienda, et pro sententia, ac voluntate sic ratione regulata, non pro incertæ rei inquisitione, ut in nobis.
anchorLine: Κύριος, ἀλλ᾽ ἡ θέλησις, ἢ βούλησις (e), ἡ ἐνέργεια
en: On 'But the θέλησις, the βούλησις': This is said by Athanasius, book 1 On the Incarnation of Christ, p. 631, with reference to that place of Paul, Romans xi, 'Who has known the mind of the Lord?' For he adds: the mind of the Lord is not yet the Lord; but it is the Lord's θέλησις, the βουλή (so it is printed there), the activity directed to something. By this he signifies that, in Paul, the word does not mean the Lord himself, nor the divine Mind that the Apollinarians wanted to subsist in him, or the Word, who would fulfil in him the office of mind; but the very power of willing and understanding, or even of acting, in relation to something. The passage of Clement in the sixth Stromata has not turned up, unless it has escaped notice through its length. βούλησις seems to mean willing which rests on a settled judgment about something; hence εὔλογος ὄρεξις (reasonable desire), and βουλή is not far off, and Athanasius could use one word in place of the other. In God βουλή is to be taken without imperfection, and for judgment and a will so governed by reason, not for inquiry into an uncertain matter as in us.

text: (f) Θέλων ὑπήκουσε. Ordo peccati Adæ; præbuit aurem uxori ad audiendum, et in ea serpenti: hinc volens, uxorisque ductus complacentia ac rei curiositate, fructum aspexit et consideravit, tum demum voluntate, ejusque consensu, comedit. Sic πρωτοπαθὴς voluntas; in reatu prima, ac peccati labe, ipsa sibi ejus auctor ac homini: quam ideo primam decuit assumi et sanari: quæ Patrum communis argumentatio est contra Apollinaristas, præque ipsorum radices stolonem, Monothelitas. Ὑπήκουσε hic quod Turr. reddit obedivit, non satis aptum, cum videatur respicere Deum, cui Adamus eo sensu non ὑπήκουσε: obedivit, sed παρήκουσε: inobediens fuit.
anchorLine: ἐξηκουσε (f), καὶ θέλων ἐθεώρησε, καὶ θελήσας ἔφα-
en: On 'willing, he obeyed': The order of Adam's sin: he lent his ear to his wife to hear, and in her to the serpent; hence willing, and led by complacency toward his wife and by curiosity about the thing, he looked at the fruit and considered it, and then with will and its consent he ate. So the will is 'first-suffering' (πρωτοπαθής): first in guilt and in the stain of sin, itself its own author both to itself and to the man; and for that reason it was fitting that it be the first assumed and healed. This is the common argument of the Fathers against the Apollinarians, and at once against the root and stem of the Monothelites themselves. As to 'ὑπήκουσε' here, which Turrianus rendered 'obeyed': not quite apt, since it seems to look to God, to whom Adam in this sense did not obey (ὑπήκουσε) but disobeyed (παρήκουσε): he was disobedient.

text: (g) Τῆς βασιλίδος. Male quibusdam additum ταύτης: indicat enim ea particula, quasi res Byzantii gereretur: aut indicare videtur. Τῆς συγκλήτου magis probo. Erat enim istud secretum, solemne concilium præsente imperatore atque senatu; quo sic Pyrrhus susceptum Mennæ libellum a Vigilio, eique lectum, mentiebatur.
anchorLine: τῆς βασιλίδος (g), ἓν θέλημα ἔχοντα
en: On 'of the queen city': 'ταύτης' ('of this') has been wrongly added by some; for that particle indicates, as it were, that the affair was being conducted at Byzantium, or seems to indicate it. I prefer 'Τῆς συγκλήτου' ('of the senate'). For that was a secret, a solemn council in the presence of the emperor and the senate; in which Pyrrhus was thus lying that Menna's libellus had been received by Vigilius and read to him.

text: (h) Ὅτι ὑπηγορεύθη. Accepisse videtur Maximus pro eo quod est in dicta epist. relata in vi synodo, act. 12. Τὸν προσφωνηθέντα λόγον Βιγιλίῳ ἐνταῦθα παρόντι. Sermonem acclamatorium Vigilio hic præsenti; id est, illi nuncupatum, quod et reddidi; exponitque idem Sergius in fine epistolæ, ubi narrat injunxisse Heraclium, cum Edessæ versaretur, ut excerptas ex illo libello Patrum auctoritates, de una Christi operatione unaque voluntate ad se mitteret. Τὰς ἐμφερομένας τῷ γενομένῳ, ὡς εἴρηται, παρὰ τοῦ ἐν ἁγίοις Μηνᾶ, πρὸς τὸν ἁγιώτατον Βιγίλιον δογματικῷ, περὶ μιᾶς ἐνεργείας καὶ ἑνὸς θελήματος, λόγῳ: ut paterna illi testimonia deflloremus, quæ continentur in libro dogmatico (sicut dictum est) facto a sanctæ memoriæ Mena ad sanctissimum Vigilium, de una operatione et una voluntate. Acclamatorius ergo sermo Vigilio, et ad Vigilium factus, idem Sergio, ἐπαγορευθείς Maximo: illi nuncupatus; quodque Maximus negat haberi in ea epistola fuisse porrectum, ἐπιδοθέντα: eamque tamen vocem illa habeat, priore loco Epistolæ, προσφωνηθέντα καὶ ἐπιδοθέντα παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ ἐνταῦθα παρόντι Βιγιλίῳ· Dirigentes etiam sermonem acclamatorium Menæ sanctissimi quondam patriarchæ hujus a Deo conservandæ Urbis, porrectum ab eo hic præsenti Vigilio sanctæ memoriæ; alterum dicamus necesse est, vel memoria lapsum Maximum, vel corruptam Sergii epistolam. Ac primum in re sic gravi ac præsenti negotio ascribere viro accurato, durius est, præsertim acquiescente ei adversario, etsi fatetur et ipse memoriam non tenere. Subdititiam vero illam vocem in Sergii epistola indicio esse potest, quod repetendo in fine, ejus non meminit, sed unam vocem habet priori illi respondentem, uti dictum est, γενομένῳ. Alter ergo editum et nuncupatum; alter etiam porrectum, solemnique conventu coram principe ac senatu lectum ac publicatum seu præsentatum dicit: quæ pugnantia Maximus arguit; tanquam scilicet non tacituro Sergio; si hæc quoque facta essent, ut receptum a Vigilio libellum, eique probatum, ostenderet: quod Pyrrhus salagebat, suo hoc plagio, a Maximo detecto: sive alias verus Menæ liber est, sive a Monothelitis confictus, eique suppositus. Turr. quod τὸ ὑπηγορεύθη reddit commonefactum de illo libello, longe est a fide boni interpretis.
anchorLine: Ὑπηγορεύθη (h) μὲν, οὐκ ἐπεδόθη δὲ
en: On 'that it was dictated': Maximus seems to have taken it from what is in the said letter, as reported in the sixth synod, act 12: 'the address delivered to Vigilius, who was present here'. That is, 'the acclamatory discourse [addressed] to Vigilius, here present'; that is, dedicated to him, as I also rendered it; and Sergius himself explains it at the end of the letter, where he tells that Heraclius, while he was staying at Edessa, had ordered that the authorities of the Fathers excerpted from that libellus, on one operation and one will, be sent to him. [Then the Greek: 'the [passages] contained in the dogmatic discourse made, as has been said, by Menas of holy memory to the most holy Vigilius, on one energy and one will', in order that we might cull from it the paternal testimonies], which are contained in the dogmatic book (as was said) made by Menas of holy memory to the most holy Vigilius on one operation and one will. So the acclamatory discourse was made to Vigilius and for Vigilius; the same, in Sergius, was 'ἐπαγορευθείς' to Maximus: 'dedicated to him'. And as to the point that Maximus denies that it was held in that letter to have been presented (ἐπιδοθέντα), yet the letter does have that word, in the earlier passage of the letter: 'addressed and presented by him to Vigilius, present here'. 'Directing also the acclamatory discourse of Menas, of most holy memory, once patriarch of this God-preserved City, presented by him here to Vigilius of holy memory': we must say one of two things, either that Maximus slipped in memory or that Sergius's letter has been corrupted. In the first place, to ascribe this to a careful man in so grave and present a matter is harder, especially as his adversary acquiesces, though he too confesses he does not retain it in memory. That the word is spurious in Sergius's letter can be shown by the fact that, repeating at the end, he makes no mention of it, but has one word answering to the earlier one, as was said, 'γενομένῳ'. So one says it was published and dedicated; the other says it was also presented, read and made public, or presented, in a solemn assembly before the prince and the senate: which discrepancies Maximus argues, as if Sergius would not keep quiet; [asking] whether, if these things had also been done, he would show that the libellus had been received by Vigilius and approved by him: what Pyrrhus was struggling to do, with this plagiarism of his detected by Maximus; whether it is some other genuine book of Menas or one forged by the Monothelites and attributed to him. Turrianus, in rendering 'ὑπηγορεύθη' as 'was reminded about that libellus', is far from the good faith of an honest interpreter.

text: (i) Ἔτι καὶ περιών. Indicat ea expressio adhuc superstitem Honorii scribam, cum hæc Maximus disputaret: favetque quod καταφαιδρύνων τὴν δύσιν· illustrans pietatis dogmatis Occidentem, additur; etsi aliqui codices καταφαιδρύνας habent, et sequitur Turr. dum reddit, illustravit: qui et sequens λαλοῦντες, non bene imperfecto, loquebantur reddit.

en: On 'still living': That expression indicates that the scribe of Honorius was still alive when Maximus was disputing this; and it is favoured by the fact that 'καταφαιδρύνων τὴν δύσιν' ('brightening the West') is added: illuminating the West with the doctrines of piety; although some codices have 'καταφαιδρύνας', and Turrianus follows this when he renders it 'illustravit' (he illuminated); who also renders the following 'λαλοῦντες' (speaking), not well, with the imperfect, 'loquebantur' (were speaking).

text: (j) Καὶ ὃν φησι λίβελλον. Illis scite Maximus in Sergium refundit libellum Menæ dictum, tanquam is non vere Menæ esset, sed illi suppositum a Sergio, ut tum viri auctoritate, tum falsa Vigilii susceptione Monothelismum abs se disseminatum fulciret. Unde non mirum sibi in eo Sergium Pyrrhumque dissentire, cum falsum, nec sibi, nec vero consentiat. Sic in vi synodo aperte νοθείας redarguitur ille libellus, cui in omnibus Maximus præivit, etsi ejus Honorii defensionem non est amplexa; quod ejus proscriptione visum mollire Orientalium animos, quod Martinus e concilio Lateranensi, tot capitum proscriptione ex nomine, ac quibuscum suspicio esset convenisse Honorium, gravius offendisset: in quam dispensationem ipsa Romana Ecclesia consenserit, ut satis aperte indicat Adrian. in viii synodo relatus, dum agnoscit Orientales dixisse anathema Honorio, sed de consensu nostræ sedis, Romanæ, cui præsidebat. Tanta hæc Sergii machinamenta Maximo exposita, ac Sergio successori in faciem objecta, veræ sint Monothelismi origines, non quam Theophanes collationem refert Heraclii cum Athanasio Jacobitarum patriarcha, cui et Antiochenum patriarchatum pollicitus sit, si modo is synodum reciperet, et in unitionem consentiret, cujus altum silentium, præterquam illis, qui simili chronographia, verbatim pene ipsum exscripserunt. Facitque quod Heraclius ad Joann. papam in Sergium et Constantinopolitanos, omnem ejus novitatis, et editæ ejus nomine Ecthesis, refert invidiam, cujus verba refert Maximus in Coll. cum principibus in secreto. Putemque incidisse Theophanem in alicujus Constantinopolitani minus probatam narrationem, quovis tandem animo hæc ille scripsisset, sive levandi causa suos Constantinopolitanos Sergiumque, sive præsidium quærendi Monothelismo, cui vir tantus, eaque zeli et unitionis Ecclesiarum specie, recepto cunctis consilio, exordium fecisset. Quamobrem etiam maluit Sergius Heraclianam Ecthesim dicere, quam suam, ejus professionis chartam, quam curasset ejus subscriptione muniri, ut ipse Heraclius auctor est. Sic sæpe chronologi, non magno judicio, hincinde aliis aliisque dicta, sæpe etiam alia aliis pugnantia congerunt; quæ omnia qui velit tueri, næ is laborem improbum casumque susceperit: potuitque mitius habere charissimus sodalis et commilito, P. Jacobus Goarius ὁ μακαρίτης in suo Theophane, quod pene tyro, non alio spiritu in eam rem, in me[...] Monothelitarum hæresi syntagmate, scripseram.

en: On 'and the libellus which he mentions': With this Maximus neatly throws the libellus called Menas's back upon Sergius, as though it were not truly Menas's but had been put under his name by Sergius, so that he might prop up the Monothelitism he had spread, both by the authority of the man and by Vigilius's false reception of it. Hence it is no wonder that Sergius and Pyrrhus disagree with each other in it, since a falsehood agrees neither with itself nor with the truth. So in the sixth synod that libellus is plainly convicted of spuriousness, in all of which Maximus led the way, even if the synod did not embrace the defence of Honorius; because it seemed that his condemnation would soften the minds of the Easterners, since Martin, from the Lateran council, by condemning so many chapters by name, and those with whom there was suspicion that Honorius had agreed, would have given graver offence: to which dispensation the Roman Church itself consented, as Adrian, cited in the eighth synod, indicates quite openly, when he acknowledges that the Easterners pronounced anathema on Honorius, but with the consent of our Roman see, over which he presided. [The remainder of the sentence is not syntactically complete as printed:] These great machinations of Sergius, laid out to Maximus and thrown in the face of Sergius's successor, may be true origins of Monothelitism, not what Theophanes reports, a conversation of Heraclius with Athanasius, patriarch of the Jacobites, to whom he promised also the patriarchate of Antioch if he would accept the synod and consent to the union; about which the silence is deep, save for those who, in a similar chronography, copied him almost word for word. And he makes Heraclius, in the letter to Pope John, throw all the odium of this novelty and of the Ecthesis published in his name on Sergius and the Constantinopolitans; whose words Maximus reports in the Dispute with the princes in secret. And I suppose Theophanes fell upon some less approved Constantinopolitan narrative, with whatever intention he wrote this, whether to relieve his Constantinopolitans and Sergius, or to seek a defence for Monothelitism, to which so great a man, with that appearance of zeal and of union of the Churches, with the plan accepted by all, had given a beginning. Therefore Sergius too preferred to call it the Heraclian Ecthesis rather than his own, a document of his profession which he had taken care to have fortified by Heraclius's subscription, as Heraclius himself is the authority. So chronologists often, with no great judgment, pile together things said here and there by various people, and often too things at odds with one another; whoever wishes to defend all this will undertake a wicked labour and risk. And my dearest companion and comrade, Father Jacques Goar, of blessed memory, could have been milder in his Theophanes about what I, almost a beginner, had written, with no different spirit in this matter, in my [...] Monothelite heresy, treatise.
